newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar says ETA may be linked to drug trade.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar says ETA may be linked to drug trade.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said on Monday there was evidence that the Basque guerrilla group ETA was partly financed by drug trafficking.

A government official said authorities may have new clues about ETA's links to drugs, prostitution and money laundering after the arrest last month of four rebels who held prison worker Jose Antonio Ortega Lara hostage for 532 days.

"If they are capable of torturing Ortega Lara in such a terrible way and of meeting their deadlines so coldly as they did with Miguel Angel Blanco, why wouldn't they be capable of financing themselves from drug trafficking?" Aznar said. "There is much evidence in this regard."
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has come under intensified scrutiny recently following its killing of Basque town councillor Blanco last month which caused a national outcry.
The government promised a crackdown on the rebels after they kidnapped Blanco and set a 48-hour deadline to transfer 500 ETA prisoners to the Basque region.
An Interior Ministry official said on Monday police and the Civil Guard were investigating new evidence that could tie ETA to the illegal businesses.
"One of those detained when Ortega Lara was freed had a number of businesses linked to money laundering," the Interior Ministry official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Spanish daily El Pais reported on Monday that authorities were investigating businesses run by Emilio Arrizabalaga Ruiz de Azua, one of four ETA commandos who held Ortega Lara captive in a tiny, damp cell. The newspaper said Arrizabalaga had real estate investments in Spain's southern Andalusia region.
Traditionally ETA has been influenced by Roman Catholic teachings and has in the past killed drug dealers in campaigns against activities it considered decadent.

Spanish authorities say the group has evolved into a criminal mafia, financing its activities through kidnapping, extortion, robbery, and the collection of a "revolutionary tax" from wealthy Basque businessmen.
The police and Civil Guard have been trying for years to dismantle ETA's financial network.
